niche.title: He Became a War Chief in World War II #shorts #ww2 #history
niche.description:
To become a Crow war chief, a warrior had to complete four deeds: lead a successful war party, touch an enemy without killing him, take an enemy's weapon, and steal an enemy's horses. Joseph Medicine Crow, the first member of his tribe to earn a master's degree, did all four as a US Army soldier in Germany in World War II, wearing war paint under his uniform and an eagle feather in his helmet. He became the last war chief of the Crow, served for decades as the tribe's historian, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2009. He died in 2016, aged 102.

During World War I, U.S. Army recruits often spent hours in processing lines for medical examinations, smallpox vaccination, and typhoid inoculation. niche.title: The Shot That 90% of WWI Soldiers Took With the Same Needle #history #medical #science
niche.description:
In the First World War, disease killed almost as efficiently as artillery — and for the first time in military history, armies fought back with mass vaccination on an industrial scale. Britain vaccinated more than 90% of its soldiers against typhoid in the last three years of the war. France went further, making typhoid inoculation compulsory for its entire army as early as 1914 — and the results were staggering: the French typhoid death rate collapsed from 118 per 100,000 soldiers at the end of 1914 to just 0.3 per 100,000 by 1917. Germany adopted compulsory inoculation just as fast.

niche.title: WHAT DID TWO WORLD WARS CHANGE IN MEDICINE? #shorts #history
niche.description:
Penicillin was discovered in 1928, but the first patient treated with it died in 1941 because the supply ran out. This Short follows five medical advances that came out of the two world wars.

Blood transfusion moved from direct to indirect, blood banks appeared, and plastic surgery grew out of facial wounds. Wartime research pushed chemotherapy forward and made penicillin mass production possible by 1944. The 1918 flu also pushed countries to build health ministries and better systems for tracking disease.

How do you put a surgeon’s experience on a printed page?

First published in 1517, Hans von Gersdorff’s Feldtbuch der Wundarznei brought practical surgical knowledge into an illustrated book written in German for surgeons working in the field. Its woodcuts helped practitioners study wounds, instruments, and procedures in an era before modern anesthesia and antisepsis.

niche.title: How Did Gedroits Treat Belly Wounds in 1904? #Shorts
niche.description: In 1904, wounded soldiers near Mukden faced a terrible choice: a risky operation or almost certain death. Vera Gedroits, one of Russia’s first female surgeons, refused to accept the old rules about belly wounds. Working during the Russo-Japanese War, Gedroits studied injuries close to the fighting and pushed surgeons to operate sooner. Her work showed what happened when doctors stopped waiting for distant hospitals. niche.title: What Roman Medics Really Did When There Was No Hope
niche.description:
Behind the roaring clash of forty thousand Roman legionaries, another battle was raging. A battle with no glory, no armor, and no modern medicine.

In this video, we step behind the lines of ancient Rome’s military machine into the valetudinarium—the field hospital. From the frontline combat medics (Capsarii) dragging mangled soldiers from the crush of battle, to the Greek surgeons performing brutal battlefield amputations with bronze saws and glowing-red cautery irons, discover the dark, gruesome, and surprisingly advanced reality of Roman military medicine.

niche.description:
#TraumaSurgery #EmergencyMedicine #USMLE

Veterans Day: what war taught your trauma bay.
Triage: Napoleon's surgeon Dominique-Jean Larrey (1790s) built flying ambulances and treated the wounded by how badly they were hurt, not by rank.
1. Stop the bleeding first: massive bleeding before the airway. In Iraq, a tourniquet placed before shock: about 9 in 10 lived; after shock, about 1 in 10. Place it 2-3 inches above the wound, never over a joint, tighten until the bleeding stops, write the time. Stop the Bleed teaches anyone.

niche.title: Why Do We Say 'Bite the Bullet'?
niche.description: Imagine a soldier on a battlefield, wounded and in agony, with no medicine and no anaesthetic — and the surgeon hands him a bullet. He bites down on it, hard, because the operation is about to begin. Before modern anaesthesia, battlefield surgery was brutal: a surgeon had to cut, or even amputate, while the patient was wide awake, so soldiers were given something hard to bite on — a leather strap, a stick, or a lead bullet. niche.title: X-Rays on the Front Line
niche.description: Could a picture save a soldier before the surgeon ever made an incision? Marie Curie brought X-ray imaging closer to the battlefield, helping doctors locate bullets and shrapnel. #History #MarieCurie #Radiography #Medicine #Technology

niche.title: Why Was Omdurman a Test for Field Surgery? #Shorts
niche.description: At Omdurman in 1898, field surgeons faced a new kind of battlefield scale. Rapid-fire weapons created waves of wounded men in the heat of Sudan. This video follows British medical officer Charles Ryan and the doctors who worked after the battle. They had to sort injuries, find water, clean wounds, and make hard choices before antibiotics or modern trauma centers existed. Omdurman shows how weapons changed medicine by changing the number and type of wounds doctors had to handle. If you enjoy early military medicine and the history of field surgery, this one is for you.

niche.title: Les Petites Curies: Marie Curie's X-Ray Vans (1914)
niche.description:
September 1914. German troops are closing in on Paris, and Madame Marie Curie boards a government train to Bordeaux with one gram of radium – France's entire research supply – to keep it safe from the war.

Back in Paris she sees the real problem: surgeons at the front can't find the bullets and shrapnel inside the wounded. So she talks wealthy friends out of their cars, has them turned into mobile X-ray vans, learns to drive and takes her 17-year-old daughter Irène along as her assistant. The soldiers have a nickname for the vans: "les petites Curies" – the little Curies.

niche.title: What Happened to Wounded Roman Soldiers?
niche.description:
A wooden tablet from Vindolanda says one in ten men in a Roman auxiliary unit couldn’t work on a given day, and only six of them were wounded. This video follows what came next for a hurt soldier: first aid on the battlefield, surgery, the fortress hospital, the decision to send him back or discharge him, what it cost him in pay and legal standing, and what he did once he was out. It also marks where the sources go silent.

niche.description:
In 1815, a wounded Redcoat lay wide awake on a door laid across 2 barrels while an Army surgeon amputated his shattered leg in a matter of minutes.

Forget the image of the cruel, clumsy battlefield butcher. At the Battle of Waterloo, experienced surgeons knew that speed was the real medicine. A leg smashed by a soft lead musket ball, taken off quickly on the same day, gave a man his best chance. Yet a single battalion of several hundred men might have just one surgeon, and around 50,000 were killed or wounded in one day.

niche.title: Brutal Surgery That Kept Rome Alive
niche.description:
Rome didn't build an empire solely with iron and discipline—its greatest weapon was what happened after the shields came down.

When young legionary Marcus is struck by a barbed arrow during an enemy horse archer ambush, survival comes down to the Roman army's frontline combat medics: the Capsari and field surgeons like Lucius. From field tourniquets to extraction spoons, honey dressings, and red-hot iron cauterization, discover the brutal realities of ancient military medicine that kept legions standing.

niche.title: How the US Army Flew Blood Across the Atlantic in World War II
niche.description:
In 1944, getting whole blood from American donors to wounded troops in Europe meant far more than loading bottles onto an aircraft. Follow the US Army, Red Cross volunteers, and military medical teams as they confronted preservation concerns, missing transfusion equipment, refrigeration challenges, and the demands of distribution near the Western Front. This World War II history explores the people and logistics behind a transatlantic medical supply chain—and why each link mattered to battlefield care.

niche.title: Did the Plasma Sent to Britain in 1940 Actually Arrive Safe?
niche.description:
Did the plasma sent from New York to Britain in 1940 actually arrive safe? Eight bottles that had tested sterile before shipping were found contaminated in England. The project's own record shows what happened next.

From August 1940 to January 1941, volunteers gave blood at New York hospitals for British patients. After the cable of November 14, a central laboratory, longer cultures and uniform rules were added. One ship, the Western Prince, was torpedoed with 222 liters of plasma aboard. The record says little about how the plasma was used in England, and this video says so.

outliers.title: The HORRORS of the Gut Wound (Why WWI Surgeons Were Ordered Not to Operate)
outliers.description:
How Survivable Was a Gut Wound in WWI, Actually?

In 1914, a British soldier shot through the abdomen got no operation. Army doctrine, inherited from the Boer War, said he had a better chance if he was kept still, given morphia, and left alone. About 4 in 5 of those men died.

This video follows the gut wound through the body and through the medical system of the Western Front: the hidden bleeding, the peritonitis, the surgeons who broke the rule in 1915, the 6 hour clock that decided who lived, and the tented hospital at Brandhoek where 126 men died in three and a half days.
